rewrites.title: AP-1 occupancy and accessibility after stimulus withdrawal
rewrites.description: Test whether AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility persist at enhancers days to weeks after a transient stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, or injury) is removed. Use time-course CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq on primed versus naive cells, and compare the sites with persistent H3K27ac and accessibility that mark memory.

rewrites.title: Causal test that retained AP-1 sites drive the second response
rewrites.description: An open chromatin site is not necessarily a functional memory element. Challenge primed cells with a second stimulus and measure nascent transcription (TT-seq, Pol II CUT&RUN, or live MS2 imaging of burst frequency and latency). Then silence (CRISPRi) or delete the retained AP-1 elements to test whether the potentiated response disappears.

rewrites.title: Pattern-dependent optogenetic AP-1 pulsing
rewrites.description: Use a light-inducible AP-1 construct (e.g., a LOV-domain-controlled Fos/Jun) to deliver pulses that vary in number, frequency, and spacing. Test which temporal patterns produce a lasting primed state and whether memory depends on pulse history rather than total AP-1 dose, i.e., whether AP-1 encodes information in its dynamics.

rewrites.title: Motif- and site-specific causal perturbation
rewrites.description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion of AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers, and measure the effect on retained accessibility and on the recall response. Compare with control enhancers that are accessible but lack AP-1 motifs, to test whether AP-1 binding at a specific site is necessary and sufficient for memory, not just correlated with it.

rewrites.title: Chromatin conformation persistence after AP-1 activity ends
rewrites.description: Perform Micro-C or Hi-C at AP-1-responsive loci at several timepoints after stimulus removal, together with live-cell imaging of locus distance in reporter lines. Test whether AP-1-formed enhancer-promoter loops remain after AP-1 is no longer bound and whether they are required for faster re-induction; loops outlasting AP-1 occupancy would indicate structural memory, and CTCF or cohesin depletion would test whether the loops are necessary.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming (degron/dominant-negative)
rewrites.description: Prime cells, then use an inducible degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during the later memory phase. Compare the secondary response (transcription, accessibility) to determine whether AP-1 is needed to establish memory, maintain it, or both; loss of memory after later AP-1 removal would indicate maintenance.

rewrites.title: Chromatin accessibility time course after transient stimulus
rewrites.description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus that induces AP-1 (FOS/JUN), such as serum, TPA or injury. Track ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and RNA-seq for days to weeks after AP-1 returns to baseline. A memory mechanism would leave persistent open AP-1 motif sites that outlast the signal; compare with naive cells to test whether the marks persist and alter a second response.

rewrites.title: Identifying which Fos/Jun dimer maintains the mark
rewrites.description: Because AP-1 is a family of heterodimers, apply subunit-specific degron tags (FOS, FOSL1, JUN, JUNB, ATF3) and deplete each only during the quiescent interval between stimulations, leaving induction intact. Pair this with CUT&RUN time courses of each subunit at memory enhancers to distinguish a continuously occupied maintenance dimer from an initiating dimer that acts transiently while the mark is kept by something else.

rewrites.title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and feedback
rewrites.description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter in single cells over repeated pulses, measuring whether history changes amplitude, timing, or the bistable on/off state. Fit mathematical models (positive feedback, hysteresis) to test whether memory arises from self-sustaining AP-1 circuit dynamics versus slow chromatin changes.

rewrites.title: Targeted erasure and decay-rate measurement at individual AP-1 enhancers
rewrites.description: After the stimulus is gone, use dCas9-LSD1/HDAC/DNMT3A tethering, enhancer deletion, or CRISPRi tiling at specific stimulus-induced AP-1-bound enhancers, and test whether the potentiated second response is selectively erased while the naive response is preserved. In parallel, measure memory half-life across a washout time course with and without proliferation arrest to determine whether decay is set by chromatin turnover, dilution by cell division, or active removal.

rewrites.title: Time-resolved AP-1 depletion during priming, rest, and recall
rewrites.description: Use a dTAG or auxin degron on endogenous JUN or FOS (or an optogenetic AP-1 switch) to remove AP-1 separately during the priming pulse, the rest interval, and the re-stimulation. Memory is expected to be lost only when AP-1 is depleted during the interval or at recall, not when depleted only during priming, giving a causal test of necessity at each phase.

rewrites.title: Lineage barcoding to trace AP-1-high ancestry
rewrites.description: Combine heritable lineage barcoding (CRISPR recorders or static barcodes such as Watermelon/FateMap) with single-cell ATAC and RNA to ask whether drug-tolerant or hyper-responsive cells descend preferentially from AP-1-high ancestors. This quantifies how many generations the AP-1 state persists and how much of final-state variance it explains.

rewrites.title: Single-cell lineage tracing of heterogeneous memory states
rewrites.description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter with lineage barcoding and single-cell multiome sequencing to follow individual cells after stimulation, asking whether memory is retained in a subset of cells with a stable chromatin state. This state should predict later responses, and its persistence should correlate with AP-1 occupancy at specific enhancers rather than with reporter signal alone.

rewrites.title: Single-cell map of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
rewrites.description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with TPA or LPS), wash out, and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN), and H3K27ac at single-cell resolution over weeks. Memory would appear as a discrete, persistent pattern of retained accessible sites that outlast the stimulus and AP-1 levels.

rewrites.title: Sister-cell comparison of memory heritability
rewrites.description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with live reporters of AP-1 activity or scRNA/scATAC, and compare sister cells after a pulse. If memory is heritable, sister cells should share response magnitude and AP-1 state more than random pairs through divisions, and the decay rate would give a persistence timescale.

rewrites.title: Acute degradation of c-Jun or c-Fos during the quiescent interval
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos with a degron (e.g., dTAG or AID) and degrade it after priming but before re-stimulation. If the primed response survives loss of AP-1 protein, memory is stored in chromatin or other marks rather than in the transcription factor; if the advantage is lost, AP-1 must be continuously present to maintain memory.

rewrites.title: Cross-context generalization of AP-1 memory
rewrites.description: Prime cells or an in vivo tissue (e.g., a Fos-based engram labeling system in neurons or a stimulated epithelium) with one stimulus, then challenge with a different stimulus, cell type, or dose. Use single-cell multiome to determine whether the same enhancers and gene modules are reused in the new context; reuse of the same primed loci across contexts would argue for a genuine memory mechanism rather than a context-specific response.

rewrites.title: FOS/JUN residence time versus persistence of accessible sites
rewrites.description: Measure single-molecule chromatin residence times of FOS/JUN/JUNB by live-cell single-particle tracking and compare them with the persistence of the accessible sites those factors create (ATAC-seq time-chase over multiple divisions). Cellular memory requires the site to outlive the factor by orders of magnitude; matched timescales would instead indicate continuous driving rather than a stored mark.

rewrites.title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation with acute AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Stimulate cells twice with a rest interval between, and measure whether the second transcriptional response is faster or larger than the first. Then use degron-tagged (dTAG/auxin) FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during the rest period, to separate AP-1 as the writer of the memory from AP-1 as its reader or maintainer.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus (necessity test)
rewrites.description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS or JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS, to remove AP-1 at defined times: during priming, after priming, and before re-challenge. Compare secondary transcriptional responses and accessibility to distinguish AP-1 as initiator of memory from AP-1 as ongoing maintainer.
